title: Homo ergaster
objectives: Describe the skeletal features associated with early African Homo erectus/ergaster.
Explain what Turkana Boy contributes to evidence about growth and locomotion.
Evaluate tool associations and disputed species boundaries.

glossary.definition: Worked on two faces, as in many Acheulean handaxes.
The classification and naming of organisms.
Referring to the skeleton below the skull.

slides.title: An early African Homo group
slides.html: Homo ergaster is a name used by some researchers for early African fossils that other researchers include within Homo erectus. The difference concerns how much variation is allowed within a species. Consequently, the same specimen may carry different labels in different scientific accounts without the underlying fossil changing. Keep the classification convention explicit.

slides.title: Body proportions and upright movement
slides.html: Early African erectus/ergaster remains show relatively long legs and shorter arms in relation to the trunk than many earlier hominins. These proportions, together with the pelvis and lower limbs, support efficient terrestrial bipedal locomotion. They do not establish an exact running speed or prove that every individual moved identically to a living human.

diagram.caption: Schematic skeletal landmarks for interpreting body proportions, not a reconstruction or measurement of a particular fossil.

slides.title: Skull and body need separate comparison
slides.html: A more human-like body plan did not require a fully modern human skull. Fossils assigned to this group can retain a long, relatively low braincase, a projecting face and no prominent modern-human chin. Human evolution was mosaic: different anatomical systems changed at different rates rather than advancing together through a fixed sequence.

slides.title: The Turkana Boy specimen
slides.html: The partial skeleton KNM-WT 15000, commonly called Turkana Boy or Nariokotome Boy, was discovered in Kenya in 1984. Its preservation includes much more of the body than an isolated skull provides. Researchers can compare limbs, trunk, teeth and skull in one juvenile individual rather than combining unrelated bones from several individuals.

slides.title: Reconstructing growth cautiously
slides.html: Because Turkana Boy was immature, researchers estimate age from dental development and skeletal maturation. Adult height estimates also require assumptions about the growth pattern. A juvenile fossil should not simply be enlarged using a modern human growth curve without testing that assumption. Individual age, sex, development and preservation affect anatomical comparisons.

slides.title: Acheulean technology
slides.html: Many early African Homo populations are associated with Acheulean stone-working traditions. A handaxe is commonly shaped by removing flakes from both faces of a core, producing a useful edge. This differs from treating every discarded flake as waste: both shaped cores and flakes may have served functions, depending on the assemblage.

diagram.caption: Schematic core, detached flake and bifacial handaxe. An archaeological association does not identify every individual toolmaker.

slides.title: What tool manufacture can reveal
slides.html: Repeated flake removal requires control of striking position, force and material properties. Archaeologists investigate planning and skill through tool scars, experimental replication and patterns of manufacture. Tool complexity alone cannot reveal a complete language system. Nor does a stone found near a fossil necessarily prove that the fossil individual made it.

slides.title: Classification remains a hypothesis
slides.html: To argue that ergaster deserves a separate species name, researchers compare suites of traits, variation, geography and time. To include it within erectus, they must explain those differences as variation within a broader species. A well-supported account distinguishes the observed anatomy from the proposed relationship to later Homo populations.

slides.title: Limb proportions connect anatomy with function
slides.html: The functional effect of a long leg is not simply that its owner is taller. During walking, longer lower limbs can increase the distance covered by a stride, while pelvis, hip, knee and foot anatomy influence balance and the transfer of forces. Examine these structures together. A fossil femur provides evidence about locomotor loading; it does not independently reveal endurance, daily travel distance or the exact speed of a particular individual.

slides.title: Separate a ratio from a body-size measurement
slides.html: A limb proportion is a comparison between measurements. In an invented example, an arm length of 60 units and leg length of 90 units gives an arm-to-leg ratio of 0.67. A second individual with lengths 50 and 75 has the same ratio despite being smaller. Ratios help separate shape from overall size, but measurement landmarks must be defined consistently and incomplete bones introduce additional estimation uncertainty.

slides.title: Why one associated skeleton is valuable
slides.html: An associated skeleton preserves anatomical relationships within one individual. Its skull, limb lengths and developmental stage can be compared without assuming that an isolated skull and a distant femur belonged to the same organism. Nevertheless, association must be demonstrated by excavation context. Researchers assess whether bones fit anatomically, have compatible preservation and occur in a plausible arrangement rather than assembling a convenient mixture of individuals.

slides.title: Juvenile growth changes the interpretation
slides.html: Immature individuals have not reached adult body proportions, and different tissues mature at different rates. Tooth development can provide an age indicator independent of the degree of fusion at a limb-bone growth plate. Agreement strengthens an interpretation; disagreement invites examination of the growth assumptions, preservation and measurement. Adult reconstruction requires a model of remaining growth rather than treating the preserved skeleton as a small, complete adult.

slides.title: Bifacial shaping is an ordered process
slides.html: To shape a bifacial implement, a knapper selects stone with suitable fracture properties, strikes flakes from one face, turns the object and removes additional flakes from the other face. The evolving edges provide platforms for later removals. Scars therefore retain a partial record of manufacture. Comparing the orientation and sequence of overlapping scars helps distinguish controlled shaping from an accidentally fractured cobble without assuming perfect symmetry.

slides.title: Classify observations before naming relationships
slides.html: A thin cranial wall, a particular brow form or a limb proportion is an observation or measurement; membership of a named species is an interpretation. Researchers evaluate whether proposed differences exceed expected variation caused by age, sex, geography and preservation. A larger sample can reveal that two apparently distinct forms overlap. This distinction explains how a fossil can remain important even when researchers revise its taxonomic assignment.

slides.title: Use this chapter to support the required comparisons
slides.html: For SCSA, this chapter supports understanding of Homo erectus and broader hominin anatomical and technological trends. The separate name ergaster is useful background rather than an additional required fossil category. In an explanation, identify the skeletal feature, link it to a plausible functional consequence, then state the evidence limitation. This three-part structure is more informative than claiming that an entire species suddenly acquired every modern human characteristic.

Flakes were removed from both faces of the core.

questions.prompt: Explain why Turkana Boy is especially valuable for studying early Homo locomotion, and give one limitation.
questions.model: The skeleton preserves substantial postcranial material, allowing researchers to relate limb proportions and body structure within one individual. These features support interpretations of habitual terrestrial bipedalism. However, it is a juvenile, so comparisons with adults require developmental assumptions. A single specimen also cannot represent every individual or population assigned to a broad taxonomic group.
criteria: Use postcranial evidence rather than the species name.

questions.prompt: Assess the claim: finding a handaxe beside an ergaster fossil proves that this species had modern language.
questions.model: A secure association may connect a population with a toolmaking tradition, and repeated manufacture can support inferences about skill and planning. It does not directly preserve speech or the full organisation of language. The fossil and artefact may also have different depositional histories. Evidence for language requires a wider argument, so the claim goes beyond what the association alone establishes.
criteria: Distinguish evidence of toolmaking from direct evidence of language.
Consider association and depositional context.
State a justified, limited conclusion.

title: Homo erectus
objectives: Recognise the anatomical pattern commonly assigned to Homo erectus.
Relate geographical distribution to dispersal evidence.
Separate archaeological observations from behavioural interpretations.

glossary.definition: Movement of a population into a new geographical area.
Bony prominence above the eye sockets.
A group of archaeological objects considered together in context.

slides.title: A widespread fossil record
slides.html: Homo erectus is known from a large geographical and temporal range. Fossils historically received regional names before many were grouped under erectus. Some researchers still distinguish early African material as Homo ergaster. Treat geographical labels and proposed species boundaries separately: similar naming does not guarantee that every population was anatomically or behaviourally identical.

slides.title: Reading the time range
slides.html: A commonly used broad range for Homo erectus is approximately 1.9 million to 110,000 years ago, although estimates depend on which fossils are included. These dates do not mean a single unchanged population occupied every region continuously. A species range combines evidence from particular sites, each with its own dating and classification uncertainties.

diagram.caption: Approximate endpoints for a broad species concept, not a continuous occupation record for every region.

slides.title: A characteristic cranial pattern
slides.html: Many fossils show a long, low cranial vault, substantial brow ridges and no prominent modern-human chin. Brain size and other traits vary between specimens and populations. Identification should compare several traits together. A large braincase alone does not uniquely identify erectus, and cranial capacity is not a direct numerical measure of intelligence.

diagram.caption: Schematic landmarks used in skull comparison; this is not a species-specific fossil reconstruction.

slides.title: Postcranial evidence and variation
slides.html: Early members of the broad erectus group had body proportions suited to substantial terrestrial travel. Long lower limbs support walking efficiency, but body size, robusticity and proportions vary. Comparing fossils requires attention to sex, age, preservation and geographical sampling. Do not infer that an entire widespread species had one exact height or mass.

slides.title: Evidence of movement beyond Africa
slides.html: Fossils assigned to early Homo outside Africa demonstrate dispersal beyond the continent. Dates and anatomical comparisons help reconstruct the sequence of occupations. A fossil establishes presence at a particular place and time; gaps between known sites do not map the exact route taken, and the earliest discovered site need not mark the earliest actual arrival.

slides.title: Technology was not uniform
slides.html: Acheulean handaxes are associated with many erectus-era populations, but tool traditions differed across regions. The presence or absence of one tool form cannot automatically define a biological species. Raw materials, activities, preservation and excavation coverage influence an assemblage. Technology is learned behaviour and can be transmitted without a corresponding change in species.

slides.title: Food and fire require contextual evidence
slides.html: Cut marks, animal remains, plant residues, use-wear and hearth-like features can inform interpretations of subsistence. Each has alternatives that must be tested: natural fires can burn sediments, and animal remains can accumulate through non-human processes. Avoid treating all erectus sites as proof of identical hunting strategies or regular controlled fire use.

slides.title: Interpreting a long-lived lineage
slides.html: A long fossil range makes erectus important for studying variation and adaptation over time. It does not turn the group into a single rung below modern humans. Researchers test relationships by combining dated anatomy, geography and archaeological context. Extinction, branching and population contact must all be considered when explaining the later history of Homo.

slides.title: Explain a skull as a combination of traits
slides.html: When describing an erectus skull, distinguish the shape of the cranial vault from the projection of the face and the form of the jaw. A long, low vault differs from the rounded vault typical of recent sapiens, while a marked brow region is a separate feature. These traits form a pattern rather than a numerical checklist: broken bone or individual variation can obscure one feature without invalidating all other evidence.

slides.title: Cranial capacity is not cerebral cortex size
slides.html: Cranial capacity estimates the internal volume of the braincase. It does not separately measure the relative size of the cerebral cortex, the organisation of neural connections or the behavioural performance of the individual. Body size also affects brain-size comparisons. Fossils preserve bone, so an endocast provides indirect information about the brain surface and overall form rather than a complete record of soft tissue or cognition.

slides.title: A dispersal claim needs both position and time
slides.html: A securely identified fossil outside Africa demonstrates that a relevant population occupied that locality. Dating places that occupation in a sequence, while comparison with other sites helps evaluate possible dispersal models. The reasoning depends on both measurements: an undated specimen gives limited chronological information, and a well-dated stone without a reliable anatomical association may not identify its maker. Several occupations can occur at the same locality.

slides.title: A handaxe is produced through repeated decisions
slides.html: Acheulean manufacture commonly reduces a stone blank on both faces. The knapper manages thickness, edge angle and the position of each strike, often using previous scars to guide later removals. Finished form reflects raw material, skill, maintenance and intended use. A roughly symmetric outline supports an argument for controlled manufacture, but identical symmetry is not necessary for a functional implement and does not directly demonstrate modern language.

slides.title: Flakes reveal more than finished objects alone
slides.html: A site containing many flakes, cores and unfinished tools can preserve stages of manufacture that a single attractive handaxe conceals. Refitting a removed flake onto its parent core strengthens an inference that manufacture occurred locally. Conversely, a finished object made of non-local stone suggests transport of material or tools, but does not establish the distance travelled by the individual whose fossil happens to occur nearby.

slides.title: Worked example: assess evidence for controlled fire
slides.html: Consider a hypothetical deposit with burnt bone and darkened sediment. Those observations show heating, but a natural wildfire is an alternative explanation. A spatially bounded feature, repeated occupation surfaces, appropriate temperatures and secure association with artefacts would strengthen a controlled-fire interpretation. The conclusion should match the combined evidence. It is stronger to describe a particular supported occupation than to assert that every erectus population routinely used fire.

slides.title: Link technology with selection cautiously
slides.html: Stone processing can change which foods or other resources a population obtains, potentially altering survival and reproductive conditions. However, a newly learned technique can spread culturally without an immediate change in allele frequencies. To claim biological evolution, an explanation must involve inherited variation and differential reproductive contribution over generations. The archaeological appearance of a tool tradition alone is evidence of behaviour, not a measured genetic change in the population.

questions.prompt: Explain why Homo erectus should not be represented as one unchanged population on a straight ladder to Homo sapiens.
questions.model: The broad erectus category includes fossils separated by large distances and long periods. Anatomical variation and regional tool traditions indicate population diversity, while fossil gaps leave relationships uncertain. Later Homo evolution involved branching and sometimes contact between populations. Consequently, erectus is a useful classification of evidence, but not proof that every included population formed one direct, unchanged ancestral line.
criteria: Explain geographical and temporal variation.
Distinguish classification from demonstrated direct ancestry.
Recognise branching or population complexity.

It does not alone establish whether animals were hunted or scavenged. The biological identity of the toolmakers also requires secure fossil association, and sediment disturbance must be excluded before treating all objects as contemporaneous.
criteria: Link cut marks and tools to a bounded behavioural inference.
Distinguish hunting from scavenging.

title: Homo heidelbergensis and Homo floresiensis
objectives: Compare the evidence associated with two different fossil groups.
Explain why species definitions and ancestry hypotheses may be debated.
Evaluate the relationship between body size, tools and ecological context.

glossary.definition: The specimen that anchors a species name.
Evolution of smaller body size in some island populations.
A geological interval important for several later Homo lineages.

slides.title: Two groups, different questions
slides.html: Homo heidelbergensis and Homo floresiensis illustrate different problems in classification. The first name has been applied to varied Middle Pleistocene fossils; the second refers to a distinctive small-bodied group from Flores. Their inclusion in the same chapter does not imply a direct ancestor–descendant relationship or that similar classification questions have identical answers.

slides.title: The heidelbergensis label
slides.html: The name Homo heidelbergensis is based on a jaw from Germany. Its wider use has included fossils from different regions with combinations of robust faces, substantial brow regions and larger braincases. Researchers disagree about which specimens belong together. A broad list of sites under one name should therefore be read as a taxonomic proposal, not an uncontested population map.

slides.title: Anatomy and proposed relationships
slides.html: Some fossils placed under heidelbergensis have been discussed as possible ancestors or relatives of Neanderthals and modern humans. Those relationships are hypotheses tested with dates, anatomy and molecular evidence where available. European and African Middle Pleistocene populations need not have identical histories, and one species name should not hide that uncertainty.

diagram.caption: An illustrative branching model, not an asserted heidelbergensis family tree. A proposed common ancestor requires independent evidence.

slides.title: Technological associations
slides.html: Prepared cores, handaxes and wooden implements at some Middle Pleistocene sites suggest skilled processing of materials. Tool form and wear can support functional interpretations. Assigning an industry to a particular species is more difficult when fossils and artefacts are not securely associated. A cultural tradition may also extend across more than one biological population.

slides.title: The Flores fossils
slides.html: Homo floresiensis was identified from fossils discovered at Liang Bua on Flores in 2003. The remains combine small body and brain size with a distinctive anatomical pattern. A species assessment compares the whole available skeleton and multiple specimens, rather than deciding from small stature alone whether the remains represent an unusual modern human.

slides.title: Dates were revised
slides.html: Later work revised the Liang Bua chronology. The principal floresiensis skeletal remains are approximately 100,000–60,000 years old, while associated stone-tool evidence extends to about 50,000 years ago. Older claims of survival until around 12,000 years ago should not be presented as established current dates. Revised stratigraphy can change an evolutionary interpretation.

diagram.caption: Approximate Liang Bua evidence ranges. A tool date is not itself a direct date of a particular fossil individual.

slides.title: Island ecology and origins
slides.html: Island environments can favour body-size changes, but insular dwarfism is an explanatory hypothesis, not a universal rule. Researchers compare floresiensis with earlier Homo and evaluate possible dispersal histories. Its exact ancestry remains debated. Explaining a small-bodied lineage requires anatomical, ecological and chronological evidence rather than assuming every small island organism shares the same cause.

slides.title: Brain size and archaeological evidence
slides.html: Stone tools associated with the Flores record show that small brain size is not equivalent to an absence of technological behaviour. The relationship between brain organisation, body size and behaviour is complex. Tool associations still need secure dating and context; they cannot reveal every cognitive ability or establish a modern-human-like language system.

slides.title: Avoid unsupported extinction stories
slides.html: The disappearance of a fossil or tool record provides evidence about the latest currently recognised occurrence, not an automatic explanation for extinction. Competition, environmental change and sampling can all be investigated. A claim that modern humans killed the Flores population requires direct supporting evidence; approximate temporal proximity by itself does not demonstrate that mechanism.

slides.title: An island is an evolutionary context, not a cause by itself
slides.html: An island can alter available food, predators, competitors and opportunities for migration. These conditions may change the relative reproductive success of inherited body-size variants over many generations. Small population size can also increase the role of genetic drift. An island association therefore suggests mechanisms to test; it does not establish that a particular lineage became small through selection rather than ancestry, chance or a combination of processes.

slides.title: Separate individual pathology from population pattern
slides.html: A proposed developmental disorder concerns how one individual grew. A species-level explanation concerns repeated anatomical patterns across a population and their relationship to other groups. Researchers compare more than height: skull form, teeth, limb joints and other structures provide partly independent information. If several individuals share a distinctive combination, an explanation restricted to one abnormal individual becomes less sufficient, although preservation still limits the available sample.

slides.title: Size and shape answer different questions
slides.html: Scaling a skeleton down preserves its proportions; evolutionary changes need not do so. A small-bodied organism can have relative limb or joint shapes unlike a scaled modern human. Measurements should therefore separate absolute size from ratios and structural features. A reconstruction that simply shrinks a modern person can conceal the very evidence that matters for classification, locomotor interpretation and comparisons with earlier members of Homo.

slides.title: The age of a layer depends on its geological history
slides.html: Cave sediments can accumulate unevenly, undergo erosion and later receive younger material beside older deposits. Apparent vertical proximity does not guarantee contemporaneity. A revised excavation can reveal an erosional boundary that changes which material dates a fossil-bearing deposit. This is why newer dates should be evaluated with the stratigraphic explanation rather than treated as arbitrary replacements for an earlier number in a timeline.

slides.title: Compare competing classifications explicitly
slides.html: A broad heidelbergensis category groups specimens thought to share a meaningful anatomical pattern; a narrower classification separates regional populations with different evolutionary histories. Either proposal must explain similarities as well as differences, dates and geographical distribution. The existence of disagreement does not make all classifications equally supported. Evaluate which fossils are included, which traits justify the grouping and whether new molecular evidence is compatible with the proposed relationship.

slides.title: Do not turn an intermediate feature into a known ancestor
slides.html: An older fossil with some traits seen in later populations may represent an ancestor, a close relative or a separate lineage retaining similar features. A direct-ancestor claim requires a compatible age and location plus a broader pattern of evidence. Older age alone is insufficient because many lineages coexist and later become extinct. Draw a distinction between a plausible branching model and an observation of an actual parent–descendant relationship.

slides.title: Use unusual fossils to evaluate a general claim
slides.html: The Flores record helps challenge the simple assertion that technological behaviour requires one fixed brain volume. Archaeological evidence must still be securely associated, and the result does not imply that brain organisation is irrelevant. For SCSA, these additional taxa supply supporting examples for interpreting fossils and models. Prioritise the specified hominin comparisons while using these cases to practise distinguishing evidence, inference and remaining uncertainty.

questions.prompt: Explain how revised dates for Homo floresiensis can change interpretations without changing the fossils themselves.
questions.model: A fossil’s anatomical observations can remain the same while improved excavation and stratigraphic analysis alter its age estimate. Revised ages change which other populations and environments may have overlapped with it. Consequently, dispersal and extinction hypotheses may need revision. A date for associated artefacts must also be distinguished from a direct fossil date, so every chronology should identify the material and method used.
criteria: Distinguish anatomical evidence from age interpretation.
Explain consequences for overlap or dispersal hypotheses.
Identify the need to specify dated material or context.

questions.prompt: Assess the claim that a small fossil body and brain automatically identify a diseased Homo sapiens individual.
questions.model: Small size alone is insufficient for species identification or diagnosis. Homo floresiensis is recognised as a distinct taxon by most researchers, although its ancestry is debated. A proposed pathological explanation must account for the full observed pattern rather than select a single small measurement.

Use multiple anatomical and contextual comparisons.
Distinguish taxon recognition from uncertainty about ancestry.

title: Homo neanderthalensis
objectives: Recognise Neanderthal anatomical and archaeological evidence.
Explain how ancient DNA changed models of population relationships.
Evaluate behavioural inferences and distinguish Neanderthals from Denisovans.

glossary.definition: Transfer of genetic variants between lineages through interbreeding and subsequent reproduction.
A stone core shaped to control the removal of useful flakes.
Genetic material recovered from remains of past organisms.

slides.title: A closely related human lineage
slides.html: Neanderthals were a distinct Homo lineage occupying parts of Europe and western and central Asia. Their record extends through a long period of changing environments, with the latest securely recognised occurrences around 40,000 years ago. They were not living chimpanzees or a simple unfinished stage of modern humans; their history was a branching part of human evolution.

slides.title: Recognising a suite of cranial traits
slides.html: Typical comparisons consider a long, low skull, strong brow region, projecting midface and features at the back of the cranium. Neanderthals generally lacked the prominent projecting bony chin characteristic of modern humans. No single trait is an infallible species label: preservation, individual variation and the combination of features all matter.

diagram.caption: Schematic locations used in comparison. This does not reconstruct a specific Neanderthal or imply that one feature alone diagnoses the species.

slides.title: Body proportions and environments
slides.html: Many Neanderthal fossils show robust skeletons and relatively short distal limb segments. Compact proportions can reduce surface area relative to body volume and are consistent with cold-climate adaptation. However, environment, activity and developmental history can all influence form. A functional explanation should identify a mechanism while avoiding the claim that every anatomical feature has one proven adaptive cause.

slides.title: Correcting an older stereotype
slides.html: Early reconstructions helped popularise a permanently stooped, awkward Neanderthal. That interpretation was influenced by particular specimens and disease-related changes. Broader skeletal evidence supports habitual upright bipedalism. A single injured or elderly individual should not define the normal posture, abilities or intelligence of an entire fossil population.

slides.title: Tools and prepared-core techniques
slides.html: Neanderthals are strongly associated with many Mousterian assemblages. Prepared-core methods control flake removal; some tools were hafted to other materials. These techniques reveal skilled manufacture, but archaeological industries are not biological species. Similar techniques could be shared or independently developed, so the identity of makers depends on wider site evidence.

diagram.caption: A schematic core and detached flake illustrate manufacture. Prepared-core traditions involve more control than this simplified drawing can show.

slides.title: Hunting, care and daily life
slides.html: Animal processing evidence, shelters, hearths and tool wear inform reconstructions of Neanderthal subsistence. Survival after serious injury can support an inference of assistance, but the exact social arrangement is difficult to recover. Evidence should be described first; behavioural interpretation follows, with alternative explanations and uncertainty stated where appropriate.

slides.title: Burial and symbolic interpretation
slides.html: Some Neanderthal sites provide evidence consistent with deliberate burial. Burial does not by itself reveal a specific religion or belief about an afterlife. Claims about grave offerings require careful excavation records and exclusion of natural processes. The strongest conclusions distinguish body placement and sediment evidence from more speculative interpretations of symbolic meaning.

slides.title: DNA and interbreeding
slides.html: Ancient nuclear DNA demonstrates that Neanderthal and modern-human populations interbred. Many living populations carry some Neanderthal-derived genetic material, though amounts and histories vary. An earlier mitochondrial comparison alone could not establish that no interbreeding occurred. Different parts of the genome retain different histories, so wider genomic sampling can revise an initial conclusion.

slides.title: Denisovans and related lineages
slides.html: Denisovans were identified primarily through ancient genetic evidence and are more closely related to Neanderthals than to modern humans. Denisovan ancestry is present in some living populations. Sparse remains make many anatomical and geographical questions difficult. It is inaccurate to treat a small number of fragments as a complete picture of a widespread lineage.

diagram.caption: Simplified branching relationship. Historical gene flow occurred between lineages and is not represented by the tree’s branches alone.

slides.title: Combining anatomy and genomes
slides.html: Morphology, dates, geography and genetics provide partly independent evidence. A branching tree summarises divergence, while admixture requires additional connections between populations. Classification as separate species does not imply that interbreeding was impossible. A strong explanation states which evidence supports divergence and which evidence supports gene flow, rather than forcing one to exclude the other.

slides.title: Compact proportions and heat exchange
slides.html: Heat exchange depends partly on exposed surface area, while body volume is related to the amount of heat-producing tissue. Relatively short distal limbs reduce exposed area compared with a more elongated form of similar volume. This supplies a plausible mechanism linking some Neanderthal proportions with cold environments. The argument concerns relative form, not the claim that every robust bone evolved for warmth or that anatomy alone reconstructs the exact climate experienced.

slides.title: A worked physical model has limits
slides.html: Two invented solid cubes illustrate the size effect. A cube with side two units has area 24 and volume eight, giving a ratio of three; one with side four has area 96 and volume 64, giving a ratio of 1.5. The larger cube has a lower surface-area-to-volume ratio. Real bodies are not cubes: shape, blood flow, clothing, activity and behaviour also influence heat exchange.

slides.title: Prepared cores separate planning from the final strike
slides.html: In a prepared-core method, earlier removals create a surface and striking platform that help control the shape of a later flake. The useful flake is therefore connected to preparation performed before it is detached. Archaeologists examine scar sequences, the shape of discarded cores and refitting pieces. Calling a tool a scraper describes an interpreted working edge or function; it does not automatically identify the complete manufacturing sequence or its biological maker.

slides.title: Hafting adds a chain of material requirements
slides.html: A stone point attached to a shaft combines materials with different properties: a hard edge for cutting or penetration and a longer support that transfers force. Adhesive or binding may secure the join. Manufacturing this composite implement involves obtaining materials, shaping parts and assembling them in a suitable order. Residues and use-wear can support a hafting interpretation, but a missing wooden shaft is unsurprising where organic material decays.

slides.title: Injury and assistance are not the same observation
slides.html: A healed fracture shows that an individual survived after an injury long enough for healing to occur. Its implication for assistance depends on how severely the injury would have limited movement, feeding or other necessities. Researchers compare several lines of evidence before inferring support from others. The stronger argument explains why independent survival was difficult; it does not simply equate any healed injury with an observed system of organised medical care.

slides.title: Ancient DNA needs controls against contamination
slides.html: Modern human DNA can enter a sample during excavation, handling or laboratory processing. Researchers use clean procedures, negative controls and characteristic ancient molecular damage to assess authenticity, then compare results across genome regions and specimens. Reproducible sequence patterns are stronger than a single short fragment. Genetic comparisons can distinguish shared ancestry and later gene flow, but each interpretation also requires suitable population models and attention to incomplete sampling.

slides.title: Compare a branching model with evidence of contact
slides.html: Divergence describes populations accumulating differences after separation; admixture describes later genetic exchange when some descendants reproduce together. These events are compatible. A tree can represent the first process, while an added connection represents the second. Nuclear evidence of Neanderthal contributions to later humans therefore refines a simple branching account without turning Neanderthals into a universal direct ancestor or implying that all living people have identical amounts of inherited archaic DNA.

questions.prompt: Which correction is appropriate when comparing Neanderthal and modern-human jaws?
options: Neanderthals necessarily had the stronger projecting modern-human chin.
Neanderthals generally lacked the prominent projecting bony chin typical of modern humans.
A chin alone measures intelligence.
Jaw anatomy cannot be compared between fossils.
feedback: This repeats an inaccurate older description.
Correct. The projecting chin is a useful modern-human comparison, considered with other traits.
An anatomical feature is not a direct intelligence scale.
Jaw features are informative when preserved and compared carefully.
questions.explanation: Correct. The projecting chin is a useful modern-human comparison, considered with other traits.

questions.prompt: What does ancient nuclear DNA demonstrate about Neanderthal and modern-human history?
options: They never shared any ancestry.
All modern humans are unchanged Neanderthals.
A mitochondrial difference rules out all contact.
Some populations interbred, producing gene flow.
feedback: The lineages share ancestry as well as later contact.
Distinct lineages and admixture do not mean complete identity.
One inherited genome component cannot exclude all historical interbreeding.
Correct. Nuclear genomic comparisons provide evidence of admixture.
questions.explanation: Correct. Nuclear genomic comparisons provide evidence of admixture.

questions.prompt: A carefully documented buried body most directly supports which conclusion?
options: Every belief of the community is known.
The individual made all tools in the layer.
The body may have been deliberately placed; specific religious beliefs need further evidence.
No natural explanation ever needs examination.
feedback: Beliefs are not fully recoverable from placement alone.
An associated body does not automatically identify every maker.
Correct. Observation and interpretation should be separated.
Alternative depositional processes must be tested.
questions.explanation: Correct. Observation and interpretation should be separated.

questions.prompt: Why is a simple branching tree incomplete for describing all Neanderthal relationships?
options: It does not automatically depict gene flow between diverged lineages.
Branches prove species could never interbreed.
Trees are incapable of representing common ancestry.
A tree’s top row gives the most intelligent species.
feedback: Correct. Additional connections or explanations are needed for admixture.
Divergence and later interbreeding can both occur.
Common ancestry is a central use of evolutionary trees.
Tree placement is not a ranking of intelligence.
questions.explanation: Correct. Additional connections or explanations are needed for admixture.

questions.prompt: Explain why a Neanderthal mitochondrial comparison and a nuclear-genome comparison can lead to different inferences about contact.
questions.model: Mitochondrial DNA records one maternally inherited lineage, whereas nuclear DNA samples many recombining ancestral contributions. A distinct mitochondrial lineage therefore does not rule out interbreeding whose detectable descendants are represented elsewhere in the genome. Larger genomic datasets can reveal introgressed segments even when a particular mitochondrial lineage is absent. Sampling, preservation and contamination control remain important when interpreting ancient genetic evidence.
criteria: Contrast the inherited histories represented by mitochondrial and nuclear DNA.
Explain why one missing lineage does not exclude admixture.
Recognise a limitation of ancient genetic sampling.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the statement that healed injuries prove Neanderthals had modern hospitals and religious burial customs.
questions.model: Healed severe injuries can support an inference that an individual survived difficult circumstances and may have received help. They do not establish a modern medical institution or a complete belief system. Burial evidence must be evaluated separately using body position, sediment history and site documentation. These observations can inform social interpretations, but precise institutions and religious meanings exceed what the evidence alone demonstrates.
criteria: State a bounded inference from injury survival.
Evaluate burial through its own evidence.
Avoid projecting modern institutions or specific beliefs without support.

Prepared-core tools and archaeological context inform behavioural interpretations.
Nuclear DNA establishes interbreeding with modern-human populations.
Denisovans are a related lineage; branching and gene flow both matter.

title: Homo sapiens
objectives: Identify anatomical features commonly used in recognising Homo sapiens.
Relate fossil and genetic evidence to African origins and dispersal.
Interpret cultural evidence without treating it as a simple species test.

glossary.definition: Still living, rather than extinct.
Use of objects or actions to represent meanings beyond their immediate physical function.
Different characteristics changing at different rates or in different combinations.

slides.title: Our species among the hominins
slides.html: All living humans belong to Homo sapiens, the only surviving species of the genus Homo. This shared membership does not mean that people are genetically or anatomically identical. Variation occurs within and between populations, and much variation overlaps. Modern populations must not be arranged as stages on a ladder from ancient to more evolved humans.

slides.title: Recognising the cranial pattern
slides.html: Comparisons often emphasise a relatively high, rounded cranial vault, reduced brow prominence, a less projecting face and a prominent bony chin. Early fossils can show mixtures of features rather than every typical modern trait together. Identification depends on the overall anatomy and context; one characteristic does not define every individual without exception.

diagram.caption: Schematic comparison landmarks, not a portrait or species diagnosis from one trait.

slides.title: An African origin with a long history
slides.html: Fossil evidence places early Homo sapiens in Africa by about 300,000 years ago. This updates older textbook accounts limited to roughly 200,000 years. Origins involved populations and changes through time, not necessarily a single sudden event at one small site. The oldest recognised fossil occurrence also remains dependent on discovery, dating and taxonomic interpretation.

slides.title: Dispersal and population contact
slides.html: Homo sapiens populations dispersed beyond Africa in more than one episode and interacted with other human lineages. Fossils, artefacts and genomic patterns constrain these histories, but no single find maps every route. Later migrations and gene flow also complicate modern distributions. Present-day location cannot simply be read as an unchanged record of the first arrival.

slides.title: Technology is evidence, not an identity badge
slides.html: Many sapiens populations used diverse stone, bone and other technologies. Blades, composite implements and carefully made small tools can reveal skilled production and particular activities. These features were not present everywhere at the same instant, and some were shared with other lineages. A species label should not be assigned solely from one tool form.

diagram.caption: Schematic flake and blade forms. Tool shape is cultural and functional evidence, not an exclusive biological-species marker.

slides.title: Symbols and archaeological context
slides.html: Pigments, ornaments, engravings and deliberately arranged objects can provide evidence relevant to symbolic behaviour. Their interpretation depends on context and alternative uses. Pigment may have practical as well as symbolic functions, and an ornament’s particular meaning may be unknown. State the observed material evidence before inferring communication, shared conventions or social identity.

slides.title: Bodies and behaviour vary
slides.html: Modern human body form reflects ancestry, development, environment and individual variation. Neither a particular body shape nor an artefact provides a simple measure of worth or intelligence. Fossil anatomy can illuminate functional constraints, while archaeology informs behaviour. These evidence types should be combined without assuming that every anatomical difference determines a fixed cultural difference.

slides.title: Biological and cultural change
slides.html: Biological evolution changes inherited population characteristics over generations. Cultural change spreads learned practices through teaching, imitation and communication, including between unrelated people. The two processes can influence one another, but they are not interchangeable. Changes in subsistence, settlement or technology can alter selection pressures without requiring every cultural innovation to originate as a new mutation.

slides.title: A modern cranial pattern does not appear all at once
slides.html: An early fossil can combine a relatively modern-looking face with a cranial vault unlike that of a recent human. Traits change at different rates and occur in populations rather than switching together in one generation. This mosaic pattern is one reason taxonomic interpretation uses the whole available specimen. It also prevents a misleading inference that any fossil lacking one familiar feature must belong to a completely unrelated evolutionary history.

slides.title: The chin is a bony structure, not facial soft tissue
slides.html: A prominent modern-human chin refers to the shape of the front of the mandible, not a beard, lip or other soft-tissue feature. When comparing fossils, examine the preserved bone and its relation to the tooth-bearing region. Missing or distorted anterior jaw fragments can make this assessment uncertain. A description of the mandible should be kept separate from the projection of the upper face and the size of the brow region.

slides.title: Blades describe a production outcome
slides.html: A stone blade is an elongated flake, conventionally longer relative to its width than an ordinary broad flake. Producing a sequence of blades can involve preparing and maintaining a suitable core. This can yield several useful edges from one piece of raw material. Nevertheless, broad flakes remained useful and continued to be made. A blade is neither an automatic sapiens identity badge nor proof that its maker had abandoned every earlier technique.

slides.title: Bone and plant materials broaden the archaeological account
slides.html: Bone, antler, wood, fibres and adhesives offer properties that stone alone cannot supply. A pointed bone implement, for example, may be shaped by grinding or scraping rather than by the conchoidal flaking used for suitable stone. Different materials require different production skills and leave different traces. Unequal preservation means a stone-rich assemblage can underrepresent the original diversity of equipment and should not be interpreted as a complete inventory.

slides.title: Composite implements reveal linked manufacturing stages
slides.html: An invented example combines a shaped stone point, wooden shaft, adhesive and fibre binding. The point must fit the shaft, the adhesive must be prepared, and the joint must remain effective during use. Damage, residues and experimental replication can test proposed functions. The existence of multiple stages supports an argument for coordinated skill and learning; it does not disclose the exact spoken instructions, social organisation or complete beliefs of the makers.

slides.title: Interpret population diversity without ranking people
slides.html: Within-population genetic variation and between-population differences arise through shared ancestry, drift, migration, mutation and selection. Which pattern is observed depends on the locus and the sampling design. Present populations are not unchanged relics of separate ancestral species, and a low diversity estimate does not indicate low human value or intelligence. A sound account distinguishes measured sequence differences from unsupported claims about the overall abilities of social groups.

slides.title: Culture can alter selection without becoming a gene
slides.html: A learned subsistence practice can change which foods are available and therefore the environment in which inherited physiological variation affects reproduction. Cultural transmission may occur rapidly between unrelated people, whereas allele-frequency change involves genetic inheritance across generations. To connect the two, identify the practice, the altered condition and the selective consequence. This causal chain is more precise than saying that acquiring a useful habit directly changes the DNA of every practitioner.

slides.title: Ethical use of human genetic evidence
slides.html: A genetic dataset can reveal information about relatives and communities as well as the person sampled. Responsible use requires informed consent, limits on reuse, secure handling and care with supposedly anonymous records that may be re-identifiable. A classroom comparison should use permitted, de-identified or simulated data rather than ask students to disclose family disease histories. Biological evidence describes variation; it does not justify ranking human groups.

The oldest fossil always has all modern traits.
A single tool always gives a species name.
Anatomical observations are never useful.

Early anatomy may contain a mixture of features.

Anatomy remains central when interpreted with context.

options: Its maker’s exact spoken sentence is recovered.
Every contemporary population used the same symbols.
It alone proves the maker’s entire genome.
It can contribute to an argument about symbolic behaviour, with context and alternatives considered.

One site cannot establish universal cultural practice.
Material culture is not a genome sequence.
Correct. Interpretation should remain tied to the evidence.

questions.prompt: How can a cultural practice spread without a new mutation?
options: It must first become a chromosome.
People can learn it from others, including unrelated individuals.
Every innovation requires a new allele in every participant.
Cultural transmission is impossible between populations.

Correct. Social learning transmits cultural information.
Learning does not require a new mutation in each learner.
Contact can transmit cultural practices across population boundaries.

questions.prompt: Explain why the phrase “modern humans evolved in Africa” is compatible with later admixture outside Africa.
questions.model: An African origin describes the evolutionary emergence of the lineage, while admixture describes later genetic exchange with other populations. A lineage can originate in one region, disperse and then interbreed elsewhere. Fossils and genomic evidence therefore address related but different events. This model does not require complete genetic replacement of every earlier population, nor independent origins of living human species in separate regions.
criteria: Separate origin from later contact.
Describe dispersal followed by interbreeding.
Avoid equating African origin with strict zero-admixture replacement.

questions.prompt: Describe how evidence for symbolic behaviour differs from direct knowledge of an ancient belief.
questions.model: An engraved object, ornament or deliberate arrangement may indicate shared representation or communication when its context supports that interpretation. The material can survive while its particular meaning is lost. Archaeologists must also consider practical uses and depositional processes. Consequently, evidence can support a general inference of symbolic activity without revealing the exact story, belief or spoken language of the people involved.
criteria: Give relevant material evidence.
Consider context or alternative practical uses.
Distinguish general symbolic inference from a specific recovered meaning.

Early African sapiens evidence reaches about 300,000 years ago.
Anatomical suites and context support identification.
Learned cultural change and inherited biological evolution are distinct but interacting.

title: Dating Hominin Fossils
objectives: Choose dating methods appropriate to the material and question.
Interpret stratigraphic brackets and radioactive half-lives.
Distinguish age evidence from dietary, mobility and climate proxies.

glossary.definition: Study of the order and relationships of layers.
Adjustment against independent reference information to improve an estimate.
Time required for half the parent radioactive atoms in a closed population to decay.

slides.title: The dated event must be identified
slides.html: A reported age is meaningful only when the dated material and event are clear. A bone’s organic component, a volcanic crystal and sediment deposition can record different events. Dating an associated layer is not identical to directly dating a fossil. Context connects the measurement to the archaeological question, and the connection itself must be justified.

slides.title: Relative ordering from layers
slides.html: In an undisturbed sequence, lower deposited layers are older than those above. This relative ordering can place a fossil before or after another event without supplying a calendar age. Faulting, folding, erosion or redeposition can disturb a simple sequence. A fossil moved from an older layer may be older than the sediment currently surrounding it.

diagram.caption: A schematic undisturbed sequence. Ages for suitable volcanic material may bracket deposition of the fossil-bearing layer.

slides.title: Comparative fluorine evidence
slides.html: Buried bone can acquire fluorine from groundwater. Comparing bones exposed to sufficiently similar local conditions may help assess relative age or whether they share a burial history. Uptake also depends on groundwater and bone properties. Fluorine content is therefore not a universal clock that converts any bone concentration directly into a numerical age.

slides.title: Radioactive decay and elapsed time
slides.html: Radioactive parent atoms decay at a characteristic probability. After one half-life, half the original parent population remains; after two, one quarter remains. The fraction follows repeated halving, not subtraction of the same number each interval. Applying this relationship requires an appropriate system and an account of initial conditions and later gain or loss.

diagram.caption: Ideal closed-system decay: parent fractions after successive half-lives are 1, 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and 1/16.

slides.title: When radiocarbon is appropriate
slides.html: Radiocarbon dating measures the changing abundance of carbon-14 in suitable carbon-containing material after exchange with the environment ceases. Its half-life is approximately 5730 years. Useful dates generally extend to around 50,000 years, depending on sample and laboratory conditions. Contamination can distort results; calibration accounts for past variation in atmospheric carbon-14 rather than assuming a perfectly fixed initial ratio.

slides.title: Volcanic rocks and older contexts
slides.html: Potassium–argon and related argon methods can date suitable volcanic minerals, commonly providing ages for layers associated with much older hominin remains. They normally date mineral-system events rather than directly measuring the age of a fossil bone. The interpretation requires geological context and assessment of whether the isotopic system retained the relevant products after formation.

slides.title: Fission tracks and other clocks
slides.html: Spontaneous fission can leave damage tracks in suitable minerals or glass. Track accumulation and retention provide time-related information, but heating can affect the record. Different methods have different materials, ranges and assumptions. A long list of techniques does not mean that any technique can be applied to every specimen with equal reliability.

slides.title: Stable isotopes answer other questions
slides.html: Stable carbon or nitrogen isotope ratios can inform reconstructions of diet, while strontium and oxygen comparisons may help investigate origins or movement. These analyses usually require environmental reference values and physiological context. They are not automatically clocks. A dietary inference or a difference from local isotope values should not be reported as a direct numerical fossil age.

slides.title: Climate records provide context
slides.html: Ice cores, sediments and other environmental archives help reconstruct past climate. Their independently developed chronologies allow comparison with occupation and migration evidence. Correlation can suggest environmental pressures or opportunities but does not alone prove a particular cause of migration. Lower sea levels can expose land in some regions without creating a land bridge across every sea.

slides.title: Combining results with uncertainty
slides.html: A strong age argument uses stratigraphy, appropriate numerical methods and explicit uncertainty together. For example, a fossil-bearing layer between hypothetical volcanic dates of 1.8 Ma below and 1.6 Ma above is bracketed by those events if the sequence is secure. It is not necessarily exactly 1.7 Ma, and averaging the bounds cannot replace an independent measurement.

slides.title: Specify which biological or geological clock is being read
slides.html: A carbon-containing sample can record the end of biological carbon exchange; a volcanic mineral can record the establishment of an isotopic system during a geological event. These events need not occur at the same time as a fossil organism died. The first step in selecting a method is therefore to identify the material and its relationship to the target event. A precise laboratory result cannot repair an incorrect archaeological association.

slides.title: Worked example: bracket rather than average
slides.html: In a hypothetical undisturbed sequence, a lower volcanic layer is dated to 1.9 million years and an upper layer to 1.7 million years. A fossil deposited between them must be younger than the lower event and older than the upper event, if both associations are secure. Its interval is therefore 1.7–1.9 million years. Reporting exactly 1.8 million years would turn the midpoint into an unjustified measurement.

slides.title: Radiocarbon contamination can bias the inferred age
slides.html: When a very old carbon sample contains little carbon-14, even a small addition of relatively recent carbon can noticeably change its measured ratio. Under a simple model this can make the sample appear younger. Conservation chemicals, roots and handling are potential sources that must be assessed, and laboratory pretreatment aims to isolate suitable material. Method choice and sample history matter alongside the numerical precision reported by the instrument.

slides.title: Repeated halving links a proportion with elapsed time
slides.html: If an ideal closed sample retains 6.25% of its original radioactive parent, the remaining fraction is one sixteenth. Four halvings connect the initial amount to that fraction: one half, one quarter, one eighth and one sixteenth. Elapsed time is therefore four half-lives under the model. This is different from treating 6.25% as the percentage of a half-life or subtracting a fixed amount of parent in each interval.

slides.title: Potassium–argon requires an appropriate mineral system
slides.html: In appropriate volcanic material, the potassium–argon system provides information about the time since the relevant mineral system formed and retained its decay products. Argon can be lost or excess argon can complicate interpretation, so geological assessment matters. A volcanic layer associated with a fossil can constrain deposition if their relationship is understood. Applying the method to suitable rock is different from claiming to date a fossil directly by measuring its bones.

slides.title: Precision and accuracy do not mean the same thing
slides.html: A method can give tightly clustered repeat measurements but still estimate the wrong event, or be systematically biased by contamination or calibration. Precision concerns the closeness of repeated results; accuracy concerns closeness to an appropriate reference or true value. Independent methods that agree within stated uncertainty can strengthen a chronology, especially when they rely on different assumptions. Averaging incompatible dates without explaining their materials and contexts can hide a problem.

slides.title: An age argument needs both measurements and context
slides.html: A useful explanation states the dated material, the method, the event represented and the uncertainty or range. It then links that event to the fossil through stratigraphy or a secure association. Relative evidence checks the ordering while numerical dating supplies time constraints. For SCSA, stratigraphy, index fossils, radiocarbon and potassium–argon applications and limitations are priorities; additional clocks are supporting examples rather than interchangeable methods suitable for every find.

slides.title: Sampling must preserve evidence and respect people
slides.html: Dating may require removing or destroying a small part of a specimen, so the scientific benefit must be weighed against conservation and cultural responsibilities. Researchers document the original context, minimise sampling and obtain the relevant permissions. Work involving human remains requires appropriate ethical oversight and respectful engagement with descendant communities and relevant Traditional Custodians. A precise measurement does not excuse an unethical collection method or a lost archaeological context.

The fossil is younger than both layers.
The ash directly measures the fossil’s birth date.

Replacing all stratigraphic observations

Numerical dates still require context.

Secure associated layers can constrain fossil context, but their ages should not simply be relabelled as direct fossil measurements.

Independent stratigraphic checks strengthen the conclusion.

title: Models for Human Evolutionary Trees
objectives: Interpret branching as common ancestry rather than progress.
Compare anatomical, nuclear, mitochondrial and Y-linked evidence.
Explain why sampling and gene flow can require model revision.

glossary.definition: An ancestor and all its descendants.
A branching history inferred for a particular genetic region.
A model of the branching history of populations or species.

slides.title: A tree is a relationship model
slides.html: An evolutionary tree proposes patterns of shared ancestry. A branching point represents a common ancestral population, not necessarily a named fossil specimen. The order of branch connections matters; the position of a tip on the left or right does not rank species by intelligence or worth. Several related lineages can exist at the same time.

slides.title: Fossils test proposed branches
slides.html: Researchers compare anatomical characters, geographical context and reliable ages. A fossil may combine ancestral and derived traits, making placement uncertain. Absence from an incomplete fossil record is not evidence that a population never existed. Proposed direct ancestry requires more support than an older date and one feature resembling a later species.

slides.title: Measurement and imaging
slides.html: Measurements help compare size and shape, while CT imaging can reveal internal structures without cutting through an entire fossil. Surface microscopy can investigate wear or marks. Each technique addresses a defined question and has limits, including distortion and reconstruction choices. Digital visualisation does not eliminate uncertainty or turn an incomplete specimen into a complete original.

slides.title: Nuclear DNA samples many histories
slides.html: Nuclear DNA is inherited from both parents and is reshuffled by recombination. Comparisons across many regions can inform population divergence, relatedness and admixture. However, different regions may retain different histories. Preservation and modern contamination are major issues in ancient DNA, and conclusions should consider the amount and quality of recovered sequence rather than only its age.

slides.title: Mitochondrial and Y-linked lineages
slides.html: Mitochondrial DNA usually tracks a maternal line, while suitable non-recombining Y-chromosome regions track a paternal line in people carrying a Y chromosome. These are informative but narrow genealogical routes, not the whole ancestry of a population. The relevant evidence is DNA sequence variation; a Y chromosome is not itself an amino acid sequence.

slides.title: A common ancestor is not the only ancestor
slides.html: The most recent common maternal ancestor of sampled mitochondrial lineages was not the only woman alive at that time, nor the sole ancestor of all human genes. Other individuals can contribute ancestry through different routes. Genealogical lineages can disappear through chance even when descendants persist through other branches of the family network.

slides.title: Branching and admixture
slides.html: A simple tree can show that two groups share a more recent ancestor with each other than with an outgroup. Historical interbreeding adds connections that a tree alone does not display. Human evolutionary models therefore may need both branching relationships and gene-flow information. Neither genetic mixing nor incomplete lineage sorting should be confused with a ladder of progress.

diagram.caption: A simplified branching relationship. Gene flow between these and other populations requires additional evidence and connections.

slides.title: Why models change
slides.html: New fossils, revised dates and improved genetic sampling can support or weaken particular branch placements. Scientific revision does not mean that every previous observation was false. It means that the explanatory model is being tested against a wider evidence base. State which connection changed and what new information justified the change, rather than saying the whole evolutionary history was reset.

diagram.caption: Evidence streams constrain a model together. The sequence is a simplified workflow, not a guarantee that every fossil preserves DNA.

slides.title: Read common ancestry at nodes, not by tip spacing
slides.html: For three groups, the pair joined by a more recent common node are sister groups in that model. Their names may be drawn close together or far apart without changing the relationship. Likewise, rotating branches around a node changes the diagram’s appearance but preserves its connections. Unless a scale is supplied, branch length should not be read as time, amount of DNA change or degree of evolutionary advancement.

slides.title: A fossil age does not itself place a branching event
slides.html: The earliest discovered fossil of a group supplies a minimum indication of its known presence, subject to dating and identification. The population that gave rise to it can predate that specimen. A divergence between lineages may be inferred from several kinds of evidence rather than directly dated by one fossil. Consequently, a branching point should not automatically be labelled with the age of the oldest available skull.

slides.title: Shared derived traits are more informative than general similarity
slides.html: A character inherited from a remote common ancestor can be shared by many groups and may contribute little to distinguishing recent relationships. A shared derived character, considered in a wider comparison, can provide more specific evidence of a closer grouping. Similarity can also arise independently or be altered by reversal. Evaluate a suite of characters and independent evidence rather than counting every superficially similar feature as an equally informative relationship marker.

slides.title: Sampling changes what a genetic comparison can establish
slides.html: A sequence comparison represents the specimens and genome regions actually sampled. A small modern sample may miss rare variants, while ancient material may preserve only short fragments. Results should therefore state what was compared and which regions were excluded because of poor quality or uncertain alignment. Agreement across independent regions and specimens strengthens an inference, but different genetic histories can still be expected when recombination and historical gene flow occurred.

slides.title: A maternal lineage is only one path through a pedigree
slides.html: A person has two parents, four grandparent positions and many more genealogical paths farther back, although ancestors can occupy more than one position. Mitochondrial inheritance usually follows just the mother-to-child route through this network. It is therefore possible for a population to contribute nuclear ancestry while its particular mitochondrial lineages are lost. Absence of those mitochondrial lineages today does not, by itself, show that no ancient interbreeding occurred.

slides.title: A network can add information to a tree
slides.html: A branching model summarises a pattern of divergence. An added cross-connection can represent gene flow between populations whose histories had already separated. Such a network communicates why a single strict tree cannot display every part of human genomic history. This does not mean all branch relationships disappear; it means the model includes both divergence and contact. The evidence supporting a cross-connection must be distinguished from the drawing itself.

slides.title: Evaluate a revision by identifying the changed claim
slides.html: Suppose a new, securely dated fossil extends the known range of a lineage. That may alter a proposed overlap or dispersal sequence without changing its anatomical measurements or invalidating all older evidence. A useful evaluation identifies which prediction is affected and which observations remain supported. For SCSA, practise interpreting supplied trees and evidence: constructing a phylogenetic tree is not required, and a neat diagram should never substitute for a justified evolutionary explanation.

questions.prompt: Correct the statement: mitochondrial Eve was the only woman alive and supplied every gene in all living humans.
questions.model: The label refers to a common ancestor of particular surviving maternal mitochondrial lineages, not the only woman of her time. Other women and men can contribute to nuclear ancestry through different genealogical paths. Some maternal lines cease to be represented without eliminating all descendants. Consequently, a mitochondrial common ancestor is a locus-specific genealogical inference, not a claim of a one-woman population or sole origin of every gene.

questions.model: An anatomical tree groups fossils using measured characters and assumptions about their evolution, while genetic comparisons use inherited sequence variation and particular evolutionary models. Both depend on sampling and can be affected by missing information. Agreement strengthens a relationship hypothesis; disagreement can prompt checks for convergence, preservation, gene flow or differing gene histories. The response should identify testable explanations rather than dismiss one evidence type by default.
